mainTopic: Climbing trees and walking on grass on שבת; consent and kindness in marriage; חוה's curses and lessons from animals
overview: This amud finishes the discussion of climbing trees on שבת. Two ברייתות disagree about a dry tree, and the גמרא concludes that a dead tree may be climbed in summer, when it is obviously dead, but not in the rainy season. It then narrows the permission to a tree with no fruit and no twigs, and explains that רב's stricter ruling in אפסטיא was a local fence. Next, רב אסי forbids walking on grass on שבת based on 'וְאָץ בְּרַגְלַיִם חוֹטֵא'. The גמרא then gives a ladder of answers to reconcile two ברייתות on this, and rules that following רבי שמעון it is permitted in every case. The same verse is then read as forbidding a husband to force his wife. רבי יוחנן praises a wife who asks for the marital מצוה, proving it from לאה and יששכר. The גמרא reconciles this with חוה's curses, explains how the ten curses are counted, and ends with lessons in proper conduct learned from animals, especially the rooster.

steps.title: Staying in the tree is itself a violation, so he must come down
steps.stepSummary: This line finishes an answer from the previous section. In the other case being compared, sitting still involves no wrongdoing. Here, staying in the tree is an ongoing איסור, so he should come down.
steps.simpleTranslation: [There it is different,] because he is not doing anything forbidden. But here, where he is doing something forbidden, he really should come down.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer that started in the previous section. It explains why a person up a tree on שבת should climb down, even though in another case the rule was to stay put.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually it is better to sit still (שב ואל תעשה) than to take an action. But a person sitting in a tree is still using the tree at every moment, and that use is itself the איסור. So staying put does not keep him out of trouble. Coming down is the way to stop the violation.

keyTerms.meaning: indeed, so too, that is correct

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new topic starting here. It is the second half of an answer that began earlier, so the word 'there' refers to a case mentioned earlier.

phrases.english: [there it is different,] since he is not committing a transgression,
phrases.notes: He means the case we were comparing to before, where just doing nothing isn't doing anything wrong.

phrases.english: but here, where he is committing a transgression,
phrases.notes: Every moment he stays in the tree, he is still using it.

phrases.english: indeed, he should come down.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes an answer begun earlier by setting a case of passive non-violation against the ongoing violation of staying in a tree.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (חילוק): passive staying with no איסור versus passive staying that is itself an ongoing איסור
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since sitting still is normally preferred, one might think the person should stay in the tree.
steps.terutzMaskana: Staying in the tree is an ongoing use of the tree, which is itself forbidden, so he must come down.

steps.title: Two ברייתות disagree about climbing a dry tree
steps.stepSummary: One ברייתא forbids climbing both green and dry trees. Another ברייתא limits the ban to green trees and permits dry ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: One ברייתא taught: both a green tree and a dry tree [are forbidden to climb]. Another ברייתא taught: when is this said? For a green tree. But a dry tree is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets two ברייתות side by side that seem to contradict each other about a dry tree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban on climbing trees on שבת is a rabbinic safeguard, so that a person does not come to tear off a branch or leaf. The first ברייתא applies it to every tree. The second says a dry tree is fine, perhaps because there is nothing growing on it to tear off. The גמרא now needs to explain how both can be true.

keyTerms.meaning: in what case are these words said? (introduces a limitation)

phrases.english: It was taught in one [baraita]:

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד אִילָן לַח וְאֶחָד אִילָן יָבֵשׁ,
phrases.english: both a green tree and a dry tree [are forbidden to climb],
and it was taught in another [baraita]:
in what case are these words said? With a green [tree],
but with a dry [tree], it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנֵי חֲדָא: אֶחָד אִילָן לַח וְאֶחָד אִילָן יָבֵשׁ, וְתַנְיָא אִידַּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: whether the tree-climbing ban covers dry trees.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two ברייתות about climbing a dry tree on שבת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One source forbids a dry tree and the other permits it, which looks like a direct contradiction.

steps.title: רב יהודה: it depends whether the stump grows back
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה answers that the ברייתא forbidding a dry tree means one whose stump still sprouts new shoots. The ברייתא permitting it means one whose stump does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: There is no difficulty. Here, it is where its stump sends out new shoots. There, it is where its stump does not send out new shoots.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה settles the contradiction by saying each ברייתא is talking about a different kind of 'dry' tree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב יהודה, a tree that looks dry but whose stump can still sprout is forbidden, because it is still alive in some way. A tree whose stump will never sprout again is truly dead, so it is permitted. In his reading, the first ברייתא is about the sprouting tree and the second is about the completely dead one.

keyTerms.meaning: it is not difficult (introduces an answer)
here... there (each source refers to a different case)
renews itself, sends out new shoots

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: it is not difficult:
here, where its stump sends out new shoots,
phrases.notes: The ברייתא that forbids even a dry tree.

phrases.english: there, where its stump does not send out new shoots.
phrases.notes: The ברייתא that permits a dry tree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction from step 2 by giving each ברייתא a different case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each ברייתא refers to a different kind of dry tree
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתות seemed to disagree about the same dry tree.
steps.terutzMaskana: A 'dry' tree whose stump still sprouts is forbidden. One whose stump does not sprout is permitted.

steps.title: A tree that grows back cannot be called dry
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that a tree whose stump still sprouts is not dry at all, so רב יהודה's answer does not fit the ברייתא's wording.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do you call a tree whose stump sends out new shoots 'dry'?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב יהודה's answer as unrealistic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא specifically says 'a dry tree.' A tree that still grows new shoots is alive, so it would count as green, not dry. That means רב יהודה's case cannot be what the ברייתא meant by a dry tree.

phrases.english: [A tree whose] stump sends out new shoots, you call it dry?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב יהודה's answer from step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's reading that the forbidden 'dry' tree is one whose stump sprouts
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A sprouting tree is alive, so calling it 'dry' goes against the plain wording of the ברייתא.

steps.title: Summer versus rainy season
steps.stepSummary: The final answer is that both ברייתות speak about a truly dead tree. In summer it is permitted, because it is obviously dead. In the rainy season it is forbidden, because people cannot tell dead trees from living ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, there is no difficulty. Here, it is in the summer. There, it is in the rainy season.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops רב יהודה's answer and gives a new one: the difference between the ברייתות is the time of year.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In summer, living trees are full of leaves, so a bare tree is clearly dead and climbing it looks harmless. In the rainy season, many living trees are also bare, so people watching could not tell the difference. They might think climbing any tree is allowed. So the ברייתא that permits a dry tree means summer, and the ברייתא that forbids it means the rainy season.

keyTerms.meaning: rather (drops the previous answer and offers a new one)

steps.whatToRemember: A completely dead tree may be climbed on שבת in summer, when it is clearly dead. It may not be climbed in the rainy season, when it looks the same as a living tree that has shed its leaves.
steps.confusionAlert: The order of 'here' and 'there' does not match the order the ברייתות were quoted. The first 'here' (summer) refers to the permitting ברייתא, which was quoted second.

phrases.english: Rather, it is not difficult:
here, in the summer,
phrases.notes: The ברייתא that permits a dry tree, since in summer it is obviously dead.

phrases.english: there, in the rainy season.
phrases.notes: The ברייתא that forbids a dry tree, since in winter dead and living trees look alike.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָא קַשְׁיָא: כָּאן בִּימוֹת הַחַמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רב יהודה's rejected answer with a new resolution to the contradiction from step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting by time of year (אוקימתא) based on how things look to onlookers (מראית עין)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The difference between the ברייתות depended on whether the stump sprouts.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both ברייתות speak about a truly dead tree. The difference is whether its deadness is obvious, which depends on the season.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A dead tree is permitted to climb in summer and forbidden in the rainy season.

steps.title: But in summer, old fruit could fall off
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the summer leniency. Even a dead tree may still hold old fruit that would fall when he climbs.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the summer, the fruits will fall off!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from Step 5, which allowed climbing a dead tree in the summer. It points out that leftover fruit might fall off when he climbs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 said summer is fine because everyone can see the tree is dead. The problem raised here is different: old fruit still hanging there could fall or be picked. That would bring back a reason to forbid climbing.

keyTerms.meaning: The summer season (literally 'days of the sun')

phrases.english: In the summer,
phrases.notes: This goes back to the summer case in Step 5, where it was allowed.

phrases.english: the fruits will fall off!
phrases.notes: Old fruit left on the dead tree may drop when he climbs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the summer leniency given in Step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that a dead tree may be climbed in summer
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Leftover fruit could fall or be picked, which raises a new concern even when the tree is clearly dead.

steps.title: The case is a tree with no fruit
steps.stepSummary: The leniency is limited to a tree that has no fruit on it.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are talking about a case where there is no fruit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the permission only applies when no fruit is on the tree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer narrows the case. If no fruit is hanging, the worry from Step 6 does not exist, so the summer leniency still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Where there is not / where there is none

phrases.english: Where there is no fruit.
phrases.notes: The permission is limited to a fruitless tree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the fruit challenge of Step 6.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any dead tree may be climbed in summer, even one with fruit.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a dead tree with no fruit on it is permitted.

steps.title: But small twigs could break off
steps.stepSummary: Even without fruit, small dry twigs could snap off when he climbs.
steps.simpleTranslation: But small twigs will fall off!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes again. Even if there is no fruit, small branches could break off during the climb.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Removing fruit from the case does not solve everything. A dead tree usually has brittle twigs, and breaking them is also a concern. So the leniency is challenged a second time.

phrases.english: But small twigs will fall off!
phrases.notes: Brittle twigs of a dead tree may snap when he climbs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge to the narrowed case of Step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The fruitless dead tree that Step 7 permitted
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Twigs can break off even when there is no fruit, so a concern remains.

steps.title: The case is a tree already stripped of twigs
steps.stepSummary: The leniency applies to a tree whose small branches were already stripped off.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are talking about a stripped tree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the case is a tree already stripped of its small branches, so nothing can break off.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is narrowed again. The permitted tree is dead, has no fruit, and has no twigs. Climbing such a tree leaves no realistic way to detach anything.

keyTerms.meaning: A stripped tree (its small branches cut away)

steps.whatToRemember: The permitted case is very narrow: a dead tree, in summer, with no fruit, already stripped of its twigs.

phrases.english: With a stripped tree.
phrases.notes: A tree whose small branches were already removed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the twig challenge of Step 8.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A fruitless dead tree that still has twigs is permitted.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a fruitless dead tree that is already stripped is permitted.

steps.title: But רב forbade even a stripped tree
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a story: רב came to אפסטיא and forbade climbing even a stripped tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רב came to אפסטיא and forbade even a stripped tree!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges Step 9 with a story about רב. In the town of אפסטיא, רב forbade climbing even a stripped tree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 said a stripped dead tree is permitted. Yet רב, a great authority, forbade exactly that case. This suggests a stripped tree is also forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: He happened to come to / arrived at

phrases.english: Is that so?!
phrases.notes: This is how the גמרא starts a question against what was just said.

phrases.english: But Rav arrived at Apsetaya,
phrases.notes: אפסטיא is the name of a place.

phrases.english: and forbade even a stripped tree!
phrases.notes: The exact case Step 9 permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the stripped-tree answer of Step 9 using a story about רב.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that a stripped dead tree is permitted
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב's ruling in practice contradicts the permission.

steps.title: רב was making an extra fence in a careless place
steps.stepSummary: רב's ban was a local safeguard for a place where people were careless. It was not the basic law.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב found an unguarded field and put a fence around it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב's ban was an extra precaution. The people there were careless, so he added a stricter rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By basic law, a stripped dead tree is still permitted. רב saw that the people of אפסטיא were lax, like an open field with no fence. So he made a protective rule for that place. The story therefore does not contradict Step 9.

keyTerms.meaning: An open field; here, a place without proper guarding
He built a fence, meaning he made a protective stringency

steps.whatToRemember: A rabbi's local stringency (a 'fence') does not change the basic law. A stripped dead tree remains permitted in principle.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not conclude from רב's story that a stripped tree is truly forbidden. His ban was a special safeguard for one careless community.

phrases.english: Rav found an open field,
phrases.notes: A metaphor for a place where people were lax.

phrases.english: and he built a fence in it.
phrases.notes: He added a stringency to protect them.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב בִּקְעָה מָצָא, וְגָדַר בָּהּ גָּדֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from רב's story in Step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reclassifying a ruling as a local safeguard rather than basic law
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב held that a stripped tree is forbidden by basic law.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב's ban was an extra fence for careless people, so the basic permission stands.

steps.title: רב אסי: do not walk on grass on שבת
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר אבא quotes רב אסי: walking on grass on שבת is forbidden. The source is the פסוק 'one who hurries with his feet sins.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר אבא said in the name of רב אסי: A person may not walk on grass on שבת, because it says, 'He who hurries with his feet sins.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a related topic: walking on grass on שבת. רב אסי forbids it and supports this with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that walking on grass could uproot or tear it, which is like harvesting on שבת. The פסוק shows that even plain walking can sometimes lead to a sin. This opens a new discussion that the next step will question.

keyTerms.meaning: He who hurries with his feet sins (משלי יט:ב)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the starting rule for the halachic question of walking on grass on שבת, which the next steps refine.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָמֵי בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַב אַסִּי:
phrases.english: Rami bar Abba said that Rav Asi said:
phrases.notes: This just tells us who is saying it; it's joined right onto the statement itself.

phrases.english: It is forbidden for a person to walk
on grass on Shabbat,
phrases.notes: He might uproot or tear the grass.

phrases.english: because it is stated:
"And he who hurries with his feet sins."
phrases.notes: Proverbs 19:2.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָמֵי בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַב אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new, related topic: grass instead of trees.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Walking on grass on שבת is forbidden, supported by 'וְאָץ בְּרַגְלַיִם חוֹטֵא'.

steps.title: Two ברייתות disagree about walking on grass
steps.stepSummary: One ברייתא permits walking on grass on שבת, and another forbids it.
steps.simpleTranslation: One ברייתא teaches: It is permitted to walk on grass on שבת. Another ברייתא teaches: It is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows two ברייתות that seem to contradict each other. It is setting up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both ברייתות speak about the same action, walking on grass on שבת. One says yes and one says no. The גמרא needs a way to make both true.

phrases.english: It was taught in one baraita:

phrases.aramaic: מוּתָּר לֵילֵךְ עַל גַּבֵּי עֲשָׂבִים בְּשַׁבָּת,
phrases.english: it is permitted to walk on grass on Shabbat,
and it was taught in another: it is forbidden.
phrases.notes: A direct contradiction.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנֵי חֲדָא: מוּתָּר לֵילֵךְ עַל גַּבֵּי עֲשָׂבִים בְּשַׁבָּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a contradiction between sources on the topic רב אסי just introduced.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two ברייתות about walking on grass on שבת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One ברייתא permits and the other forbids the same action.

steps.title: Green grass is forbidden, dry grass is permitted
steps.stepSummary: There is no real contradiction. The forbidding ברייתא means green grass, and the permitting ברייתא means dry grass.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one is about green grass, and that one is about dry grass.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction. Each ברייתא is talking about a different kind of grass.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Green grass is still alive and attached, so walking on it could uproot it, which is like harvesting. Dry grass is already dead, so harvesting does not apply to it. This matches the same live-versus-dead pattern used earlier for trees.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; the contradiction can be resolved

steps.whatToRemember: Walking on green grass on שבת is forbidden. Walking on dry grass is permitted. As with trees, the key question is whether the plant is alive.
steps.confusionAlert: The order can trip you up. The FORBIDDING ברייתא is the one about green grass, and the PERMITTING ברייתא is the one about dry grass.
steps.whyThisMatters: The same principle of living versus dead runs through both the tree discussion and the grass discussion.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this one is about green grass,
phrases.notes: The forbidding ברייתא: living grass may be uprooted.

phrases.english: that one is about dry grass.
phrases.notes: The permitting ברייתא: dead grass cannot be 'harvested.'

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא בְּלַחִים, הָא בִּיבֵשִׁים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction of Step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (each source refers to a different case)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות disagree about the same case.
steps.terutzMaskana: Green grass is forbidden and dry grass is permitted, so the ברייתות do not conflict.

steps.title: Both are about green grass: summer versus rainy season
steps.stepSummary: Second answer: both ברייתות are about green grass. The forbidding one is about the summer, and the permitting one is about the rainy season.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you want, say both are about green grass, and there is still no problem. Here it is the summer, and there it is the rainy season.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another way to remove the contradiction between the two ברייתות. This time both are about green grass, and the difference is the time of year.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the summer, green grass has seeds that your feet can knock loose, so walking is forbidden. In the rainy season the grass has no such seeds, so walking is allowed. This answer keeps the 'green grass' detail from step 14 and moves the difference to the season.

keyTerms.meaning: Or, if you want, say (introduces another possible answer)
This one and that one, meaning both sources

steps.confusionAlert: ואיבעית אימא does not mean the earlier answer was wrong. It just offers another possible way to solve the same contradiction.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say instead
both are about green grass
phrases.notes: Unlike step 14, which split green from dry.

phrases.english: and it is not difficult:
here, in the summer
phrases.notes: The forbidding ברייתא: there are seeds that may be knocked loose.

phrases.english: there, in the rainy season
phrases.notes: The permitting ברייתא: there are no seeds to worry about.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא, הָא וְהָא בְּלַחִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the contradiction from step 13. It keeps 'green grass' as the shared detail and adds the season as the difference.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since both ברייתות are about green grass, they seem to truly contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Green grass in the summer is forbidden because of seeds. Green grass in the rainy season is permitted.

steps.title: Both are about summer: wearing shoes versus barefoot
steps.stepSummary: Third answer: both ברייתות are about the summer. The permitting one is about someone wearing shoes, and the forbidding one is about someone walking barefoot.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you want, say both are about the summer, and there is no problem. This one is where he is wearing his shoes, and that one is where he is not wearing his shoes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another answer. Now both ברייתות are about the summer, and the difference is whether the person has shoes on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A barefoot person can catch grass between his toes and pull it up, so it is forbidden. Shoes prevent this, so it is permitted. The new answer takes the 'summer' case, which step 15 treated as forbidden, and shows that even in summer it can be permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: He is not wearing his shoes (barefoot)

steps.confusionAlert: Here the first הא is the permitting ברייתא (shoes) and the second הא is the forbidding one (barefoot). This is the opposite order from what you might expect.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say instead
both are about the summer
and it is not difficult:
this one is where he is wearing his shoes
phrases.notes: Permitted.

phrases.english: that one is where he is not wearing his shoes
phrases.notes: Forbidden: grass may tangle between his toes and be pulled up.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא, הָא וְהָא בִּימוֹת הַחַמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows further. It takes the summer case from step 15 as shared by both ברייתות and splits it by footwear.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If both ברייתות are about the summer, they seem to contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Walking barefoot in summer is forbidden. Walking with shoes is permitted.

steps.title: Both are about wearing shoes: a spiked shoe versus a plain shoe
steps.stepSummary: Fourth answer: both ברייתות are about someone wearing shoes. The forbidding one is about a shoe with spikes, and the permitting one is about a shoe without spikes.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you want, say both are about someone wearing his shoes, and there is no problem. This one is where the shoe has spikes, and that one is where it does not have spikes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the case again. Even with shoes on, the answer depends on whether the shoe has spikes on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A shoe with spikes or studs can catch grass and tear it out, so walking is forbidden. A plain shoe does not, so walking is permitted. The 'wearing shoes' case, which step 16 permitted, can still be forbidden when the shoe has spikes.

keyTerms.meaning: Spikes or studs on the bottom of a shoe

phrases.english: And if you wish, say instead:
both are where he is wearing his shoes
and it is not difficult:
this one is where the shoe has spikes
phrases.notes: Forbidden: grass can catch on the spikes and be uprooted.

phrases.english: that one is where it does not have spikes
phrases.notes: Permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא דְּסָיֵים מְסָאנֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows further. It takes the shoe-wearing case from step 16 as shared by both ברייתות and splits it by the type of shoe.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא) by type of shoe
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If both ברייתות are about a person wearing shoes, they seem to contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: A spiked shoe is forbidden. A plain shoe is permitted.

steps.title: Both are about a spiked shoe: long tangled grass versus short grass
steps.stepSummary: Fifth and final answer: both ברייתות are about a spiked shoe. The forbidding one is about long, tangled grass, and the permitting one is about grass that is not long and tangled.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you want, say both are about a shoe that has spikes. This one is where the grass is long and tangled, and that one is where it is not long and tangled.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its last answer in this chain. Even with a spiked shoe, it depends on the kind of grass.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Long, tangled grass easily wraps around the spikes and gets pulled out, so walking is forbidden. Short grass does not catch, so walking is permitted even with spikes. This is the narrowest case in the whole ladder.

keyTerms.meaning: Long, tangled grass that catches easily

steps.whatToRemember: The two ברייתות do not truly argue. Walking on grass on שבת is forbidden only when there is a real chance of uprooting grass or knocking seeds loose. The גמרא offers a ladder of answers, each one narrower: green grass, then summer, then barefoot, then a spiked shoe, then long tangled grass.
steps.whyThisMatters: The chain shows that the issue is never walking itself. The only concern is the realistic chance of detaching growing plants on שבת, so each answer finds a different situation where that risk exists.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say instead
both are where the shoe has spikes:
phrases.notes: Here the גמרא skips the words ולא קשיא, but the meaning is the same.

phrases.english: this one is where the grass is long and tangled
phrases.notes: Forbidden.

phrases.english: that one is where it is not long and tangled
phrases.notes: Permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא, הָא וְהָא דְּאִית לֵיהּ עוּקְצֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The final narrowing. It takes the spiked-shoe case from step 17 as shared by both ברייתות and splits it by the type of grass.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא) by type of grass
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If both ברייתות are about a spiked shoe, they seem to contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: A spiked shoe on long, tangled grass is forbidden. A spiked shoe on short grass is permitted.

steps.title: Today all the grass cases are permitted
steps.stepSummary: Since the הלכה follows רבי שמעון, walking on grass on שבת is permitted in every case discussed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And now that we hold like רבי שמעון, all of them are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the whole grass discussion with a practical bottom line. Because we rule like רבי שמעון, every case is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The five answers (steps 14–18) explained when walking on grass might be forbidden: green grass, summer, barefoot, spiked shoes, long tangled grass. All of those cases worried about grass being uprooted by accident. רבי שמעון holds that an unintended result (דבר שאינו מתכוין) is permitted, and the person only intends to walk. So in practice none of these cases is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: We hold, we rule (the accepted הלכה)
An act whose forbidden result is not intended (רבי שמעון permits)

steps.whatToRemember: All the distinctions between the ברייתות explain the opinion that forbids unintended results. Since the הלכה follows רבי שמעון, walking on grass on שבת is permitted in every case.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the five answers were useless. They explain how the two ברייתות fit together. This step only says that the final הלכה does not need those distinctions.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical הלכה: one may walk on grass on שבת without worry, because one only intends to walk.

phrases.english: And now, when we hold like Rabbi Shimon,
phrases.notes: רבי שמעון: an unintended forbidden result is permitted.

phrases.english: all of them are permitted.
phrases.notes: All the grass cases from steps 14–18.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the practical ruling after the fifth answer, making the distinctions unnecessary in practice.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Following רבי שמעון, walking on grass on שבת is permitted in all cases.

steps.title: A man may not force his wife
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי rules that a man may not force his wife in the marital מצוה, learning it from ״וְאָץ בְּרַגְלַיִם חוֹטֵא״.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא said in the name of רב אסי: It is forbidden for a man to force his wife in the matter of the marital מצוה. As the verse says: "And he who hastens with his feet sins."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic. It brings a different teaching from the same verse that was used in the grass discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, ״וְאָץ בְּרַגְלַיִם חוֹטֵא״ was read about walking. Here רב אסי reads "feet" as a modest way of referring to marital relations. One who "hastens," pushing ahead without his wife's willingness, sins.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter of the מצוה (here: marital relations)
"He who hastens with his feet sins" (משלי י״ט:ב׳)
As it is said (introducing a verse)

steps.confusionAlert: "Feet" here is a modest figure of speech, not a reference to walking. The same verse is being read in a new way.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a firm הלכה: marital relations must be with the wife's willing consent. It is part of the הלכה in the codes.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא אָמַר רַב אַסִּי:
phrases.english: And Rami bar Chama said that Rav Asi said:

phrases.aramaic: אָסוּר לְאָדָם שֶׁיָּכוֹף אִשְׁתּוֹ לִדְבַר מִצְוָה,
phrases.english: It is forbidden for a man to force his wife in the matter of the מצוה,
phrases.notes: The marital מצוה.

phrases.english: as it says: "And he who hastens with his feet sins."
phrases.notes: Proverbs 19:2. Same verse as in the earlier grass discussion.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא אָמַר רַב אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic, linked to the earlier sugya by a shared verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A man may not force his wife in marital relations.

steps.title: Forcing leads to unworthy children
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי teaches that one who forces his wife will have unworthy children.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהושע בן לוי said: Anyone who forces his wife in the marital מצוה will have children who are not worthy.
steps.whatsHappening: A second teaching on the same subject. רבי יהושע בן לוי adds what the consequence of forcing will be.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אסי said forcing is forbidden. רבי יהושע בן לוי adds a result: the children born will not turn out properly. So the prohibition comes with a spiritual consequence.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
Anyone who forces his wife in the matter of the מצוה
will have children who are not worthy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the consequence to רב אסי's prohibition.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Forcing one's wife results in unworthy children.

steps.title: The verse behind רבי יהושע בן לוי
steps.stepSummary: רב איקא בר חיננא gives the verse for רבי יהושע בן לוי's teaching: ״גַּם בְּלֹא דַעַת נֶפֶשׁ לֹא טוֹב״.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב איקא בר חיננא said: What is the verse for this? "Also, without knowledge the soul is not good."
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא supplies the פסוק that hints to רבי יהושע בן לוי's teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the first half of the same verse, משלי י״ט:ב׳. "Without knowledge" means without the wife's knowledge, meaning her consent. "The soul is not good" means the soul of the child born will not be good, which matches "unworthy children."

phrases.english: Rav Ika bar Chinnana said:
What is the verse?
"Also, without knowledge the soul is not good."
phrases.notes: Proverbs 19:2, first half of the verse.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אִיקָא בַּר חִינָּנָא מַאי קְרָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the scriptural source for step 21.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יהושע בן לוי's teaching that forcing leads to unworthy children.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משלי י״ט:ב׳: ״גַּם בְּלֹא דַעַת נֶפֶשׁ לֹא טוֹב״.

steps.title: A ברייתא confirms both readings of the verse
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads both halves of the verse the same way: the first half is about forcing, the second about repeating in a way that causes distress.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught in a ברייתא: "Also, without knowledge the soul is not good" refers to one who forces his wife in the marital מצוה. "And he who hastens with his feet sins" refers to one who has relations and repeats.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports the readings just given. It shows that a תנאי source already explained the verse this way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא confirms רב איקא's reading of the first half: "without knowledge" means forcing. It reads the second half, "hastens with his feet," as one who repeats the act in a way that causes his wife distress. Together the ברייתא backs up the whole approach of steps 20–22.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way (a ברייתא supporting the statement)
One who has relations and repeats (causing distress)

steps.whatToRemember: One verse, משלי י״ט:ב׳, teaches two things. A husband must not force his wife, and he must not act in a way that causes her distress. Marital relations must be with her consent and her comfort.

phrases.english: It was also taught so:
"Also, without knowledge the soul is not good" —
this is one who forces his wife in the matter of the מצוה.
"And he who hastens with his feet sins" —
this is one who has relations and repeats.
phrases.notes: In a way that causes his wife pain or distress.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב איקא's reading with a ברייתא, and gives the second half of the verse its own meaning.
steps.raayaObject: The reading of ״גַּם בְּלֹא דַעַת נֶפֶשׁ לֹא טוֹב״ as referring to forcing one's wife.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא explaining both halves of משלי י״ט:ב׳.

steps.title: רבא's advice seems to contradict the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא with רבא's statement that repeating relations leads to male children.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that really so? But רבא said: Someone who wants all his children to be boys should have relations with his wife and then repeat!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the ברייתא from the last step, which spoke negatively about repeating relations. It points out that רבא actually recommended repeating them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא read 'וְאָץ בְּרַגְלַיִם חוֹטֵא' as criticizing a man who repeats relations. רבא treats repeating as a good thing, a way to have sons. Both cannot be true without some distinction.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? An expression of surprise that opens a challenge
But didn't [so-and-so] say? It introduces a contradicting source
He should have relations and repeat

phrases.english: Is that so?! But didn't Rava say:
One who wants to make all his children males
should have relations and repeat!
phrases.notes: This directly clashes with the second half of the ברייתא's reading of the verse.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It challenges the ברייתא's reading in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that repeating relations is a sinful 'hastening with the feet'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא recommends repeating relations, so it cannot be inherently wrong.

steps.title: With consent versus without consent
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבא speaks about a husband acting with his wife's consent, and the ברייתא speaks about one acting without it.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not a difficulty. Here (רבא) is talking about when it is done with her agreement. There (the ברייתא) is talking about when it is done without her agreement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by splitting the two sources into two different cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Repeating relations is not good or bad in itself. What matters is the wife's willingness. With her consent it is praiseworthy, as רבא says. Without her consent it is the sin the ברייתא describes.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. This is a standard opening for an answer
Here... here. Each source is applied to a different case

steps.whatToRemember: The wife's consent is the deciding factor. The same act is praised with her consent and criticized without it.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
Here, with [her] consent,
phrases.notes: This is רבא's case.

phrases.english: there, without [her] consent.
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא's case.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: כָּאן — לְדַעַת, כָּאן — שֶׁלֹּא לְדַעַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It answers the קשיא of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each source applies to a different situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Repeating relations is either always good or always bad.
steps.terutzMaskana: It depends on the wife's consent: good with it, wrong without it.

steps.title: A woman who asks for the מצוה merits exceptional children
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that a woman who asks her husband for the marital מצוה will have children greater than the people of משה's generation.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Any woman who asks her husband for the marital מצוה will have children so great that there were none like them even in משה's generation.
steps.whatsHappening: Still on the theme of husband and wife, the גמרא brings a new teaching praising a woman who asks her husband for closeness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous steps warned against a husband forcing his wife. This teaching looks at the other side: when the wife herself wants it and asks, the result is especially blessed children. The steps that follow prove this claim from verses.

keyTerms.meaning: A matter of מצוה, here the marital מצוה

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said
Rabbi Yochanan said:
Any woman who asks her husband
for the matter of the מצוה (marital relations)
will have children
such that even in the generation of Moshe
there were none like them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It brings a new related teaching on the topic of marital relations.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman who asks her husband for the marital מצוה merits children greater than the people of משה's generation.

steps.title: In משה's generation, 'understanding' men could not be found
steps.stepSummary: The first half of the proof: משה asked for wise, understanding and known men, but in the end found only wise and known men.
steps.simpleTranslation: In משה's generation it is written: 'Bring for yourselves men who are wise, understanding and known for your tribes.' Later it is written: 'So I took the heads of your tribes, men who were wise and known.' But 'understanding' men he did not find.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts proving רבי יוחנן's claim. It first shows what was missing in משה's generation, which sets up the comparison in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה asked for three qualities: wise, understanding and known. When he actually appointed the leaders, the verse lists only two. The missing word shows that 'understanding' people, a higher level than wise, were not available in that generation.

keyTerms.meaning: People of understanding, a higher level than wisdom

steps.confusionAlert: This step alone does not finish the proof. It only shows what משה's generation lacked. The proof is completed in the next step with יששכר.

phrases.english: For regarding the generation of Moshe it is written:
"Bring for yourselves men who are wise
and understanding and known, for your tribes" (Devarim 1:13),
and it is written: "So I took the heads of your tribes,
men who were wise and known" (Devarim 1:15),
phrases.notes: 'Understanding' is missing here.

phrases.english: but 'understanding' men he did not find.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It begins the proof for רבי יוחנן's statement in step 26.
steps.raayaObject: That משה's generation lacked people of understanding
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים א:יג compared with דברים א:טו

steps.title: לאה asked, and יששכר's children had understanding
steps.stepSummary: The second half of the proof: לאה asked יעקב to come to her and gave birth to יששכר, whose descendants were 'knowers of understanding.'
steps.simpleTranslation: But about לאה it is written: 'And לאה went out to meet him and said: You must come to me, for I have hired you.' And it is written: 'And of the children of יששכר, people who know understanding of the times, to know what ישראל should do; their heads were two hundred, and all their brothers followed their word.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא completes the proof. לאה asked יעקב for the מצוה, and the son born from that, יששכר, had descendants with the very quality משה could not find.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Understanding (בינה) was missing in משה's generation. Yet יששכר's descendants are described as 'יוֹדְעֵי בִינָה.' Since יששכר came from לאה's request, this shows that her children surpassed משה's generation, just as רבי יוחנן said.

keyTerms.meaning: I have surely hired you (with the mandrakes)
יששכר, the son born after לאה's request
By their word, following their decisions

steps.whatToRemember: Proof for רבי יוחנן: משה's generation lacked 'נבונים,' but יששכר's descendants, born from לאה's request, were 'יודעי בינה.'

phrases.english: Whereas regarding Leah it is written:
"And Leah went out to meet him
and said: You must come to me,
for I have surely hired you" (Bereishis 30:16),
phrases.notes: This was her request for the מצוה. יששכר was born from it.

phrases.english: and it is written: "And of the children of Issachar,
people who know understanding of the times,
to know what Israel should do;
their heads were two hundred,
and all their brothers followed their word" (Divrei HaYamim I 12:33).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It completes the comparison started in step 27.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's claim that a woman who asks for the מצוה has children greater than משה's generation
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית ל:טז and דברי הימים א יב:לג

steps.title: The ten curses of חוה seem to oppose רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to challenge רבי יוחנן's teaching using רב יצחק בר אבדימי's statement that חוה received ten curses.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that really so? But רב יצחק בר אבדימי said: חוה was cursed with ten curses, as it is written:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new challenge to רבי יוחנן. The verse and the full attack come in steps 30–31.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge will come from רב יצחק בר אבדימי's explanation of 'and he shall rule over you': a woman asks in her heart while a man asks out loud, and he calls this 'a good trait in women.' If keeping her desire unspoken is the good trait, a woman who asks her husband openly seems not to deserve praise. That would contradict רבי יוחנן's teaching in step 26.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written. It introduces a verse

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence stops in the middle here. Step 30 brings the verse, and step 31 makes the actual point of the challenge.

phrases.aramaic: אִינִי?! וְהָאָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בַּר אַבְדִּימִי:
phrases.english: Is that so?! But didn't Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi say:
Chava was cursed with ten curses,
as it is written:
phrases.notes: The verse (Bereishis 3:16) follows next.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי?! וְהָאָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בַּר אַבְדִּימִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It begins a challenge to רבי יוחנן's teaching from step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's praise of a woman who asks her husband for the מצוה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב יצחק בר אבדימי calls it a good trait for a woman to ask only in her heart and not out loud. So how can a woman who asks her husband for the מצוה be praised?

steps.title: The first five curses: blood, raising children, pregnancy, and childbirth
steps.stepSummary: רב יצחק בר אבדימי explains the first part of the פסוק about חוה's curses: two kinds of blood, the pain of raising children, the pain of pregnancy, and the pain of childbirth.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'To the woman He said: I will greatly multiply' refers to two kinds of blood: the blood of נדה and the blood of virginity. 'Your pain' is the pain of raising children. 'And your travail' is the pain of pregnancy. 'In sorrow you shall bear children' means just what it says.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues quoting רב יצחק בר אבדימי's teaching, which it started in the last step. He goes through the פסוק word by word and lists the curses. This is the setup for the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The double wording 'הַרְבָּה אַרְבֶּה' counts as two curses: two kinds of blood. 'עִצְּבוֹנֵךְ' is raising children, and 'הֵרוֹנֵךְ' is pregnancy. 'בְּעֶצֶב תֵּלְדִי' is the pain of birth itself, taken literally. So far that makes five curses.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I will greatly multiply.' The doubled word is read as two separate things.
As it sounds; its plain meaning

steps.confusionAlert: Keep count as you go. The doubled word 'הַרְבָּה אַרְבֶּה' gives two curses, not one. This matters later, when the גמרא counts the curses and gets only seven.

phrases.english: "To the woman He said: I will greatly multiply"
these are two drops of blood
phrases.notes: The doubled verb gives two curses.

phrases.aramaic: — אַחַת דַּם נִדָּה, וְאַחַת דַּם בְּתוּלִים.
phrases.english: one is menstrual blood, and one is the blood of virginity.
"Your pain" is the pain of raising children.
"And your travail" is the pain of pregnancy.
"In sorrow you shall bear children" means just what it says.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the quotation of רב יצחק בר אבדימי that step 29 introduced.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first five curses of חוה are two kinds of blood, the pain of raising children, the pain of pregnancy, and the pain of childbirth.

steps.title: A woman asks only in her heart, and this is called a good trait
steps.stepSummary: The rest of the פסוק teaches that a woman longs for her husband but asks in her heart, while a man asks out loud. Calling this a good trait seems to contradict רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And your desire shall be to your husband' teaches that a woman longs for her husband when he is about to leave on a trip. 'And he shall rule over you' teaches that the woman asks in her heart, while the man asks with his mouth. This is a good trait in women.
steps.whatsHappening: This is where the challenge actually lands. If it is a good trait for a woman not to say her desire out loud, how could רבי יוחנן praise a woman who asks her husband?
steps.deeperAnalysis: These two parts of the פסוק bring the count to seven curses. The key line is 'זוֹ הִיא מִדָּה טוֹבָה בַּנָּשִׁים': a woman keeping quiet about her desire is praised. That seems to be the opposite of רבי יוחנן's teaching in step 26.

keyTerms.meaning: She asks in her heart, silently
He asks with his mouth, out loud

phrases.english: "And your desire shall be to your husband"
teaches that the woman longs for her husband
when he is setting out on the road.
"And he shall rule over you"
teaches that the woman asks in her heart
and the man asks with his mouth.
This is a good trait in women.
phrases.notes: This line is the real contradiction to רבי יוחנן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רב יצחק בר אבדימי's list and brings out the contradiction with רבי יוחנן.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's teaching (step 26) praising a woman who asks her husband for the marital מצוה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב יצחק בר אבדימי calls it a good trait for a woman to ask only in her heart. So a woman who asks openly should not be praised, which seems to go against רבי יוחנן.

steps.title: She shows her desire by making herself pleasing to him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי יוחנן's praise is for a woman who makes herself pleasing to her husband, not for one who asks in words.
steps.simpleTranslation: When we said she asks, we meant that she makes herself pleasing to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It explains what 'asking' meant in רבי יוחנן's teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Asking' does not mean asking out loud. It means she shows her feelings by making herself pleasant to him, and he understands. That fits both teachings: she does not ask with her mouth, yet she still makes her wish known.

keyTerms.meaning: When we said; what we meant was
She makes herself pleasing and endearing

steps.whatToRemember: Both teachings are true together. A woman should not voice her desire in words, but showing it by making herself pleasing to her husband is praiseworthy, and that is the woman רבי יוחנן praised.

phrases.english: When we said it,
it means that she makes herself pleasing before him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining what 'asking' means in רבי יוחנן's teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן praised a woman who asks her husband out loud.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוחנן praised a woman who shows her desire by making herself pleasing, without putting it into words.

steps.title: Only seven curses have been listed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that רב יצחק בר אבדימי promised ten curses but listed only seven.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are only seven!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the count of the curses. It notices that the promised ten curses add up to just seven, and it sets up the answer that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The count so far: two kinds of blood, raising children, pregnancy, childbirth, longing, and being ruled over. That makes seven, so three curses are missing.

phrases.english: These are only seven!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the list of curses from step 29 and checks the number.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יצחק בר אבדימי's claim that חוה received ten curses
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: His explanation of the פסוק only gives seven curses, not ten.

steps.title: רב דימי supplies the three missing curses
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי, arriving from ארץ ישראל, adds three curses: being wrapped like a mourner, being cut off from people, and being confined as if in prison.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came, he said: She is wrapped like a mourner, set apart from all people, and confined in a prison.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the counting problem. It brings רב דימי's teaching, which fills in the last three curses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These three curses come from the way women's lives were lived, not from the words of the פסוק. Covering her head is like a mourner's wrapping. Being set apart and staying mostly at home are compared to being shunned and to being in prison. Now the total is ten.

keyTerms.meaning: When רב דימי came from ארץ ישראל to בבל
Wrapped like a mourner, meaning her head is covered
Set apart or shunned, like someone under a נידוי
Confined in a prison, meaning she mostly stays at home

steps.whatToRemember: The ten curses of חוה are seven from the פסוק and three that רב דימי added.

phrases.english: When רב דימי came, he said:
She is wrapped like a mourner,
and set apart from all people,
and confined in a prison.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the counting problem from step 33.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adding the missing items to the list
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only seven curses can be found in the פסוק.
steps.terutzMaskana: Three more curses, from women's way of life, bring the total to ten.

steps.title: What does 'cut off from all people' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רב דימי meant by the curse of being מנודה מכל אדם.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'cut off from all people' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא picks up one of רב דימי's three added curses and asks what it actually means. This question sets up the next moves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The other two curses (wrapped like a mourner, confined like a prisoner) are fairly clear. 'Cut off from all people' is vague, so the גמרא wants a precise definition.

phrases.english: What is 'cut off from all people'?
phrases.notes: Refers back to רב דימי's list in Step 34.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of one of the three curses רב דימי just added.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The concrete meaning of the curse 'cut off from all people'.

steps.title: It cannot mean the ban on being alone with others
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the curse refers to the ban on ייחוד, then rejects this because men have the same ban.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it is because she is forbidden to be secluded with others, he too is forbidden to be secluded with others.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries out a possible answer: maybe the curse is that a woman may not be alone with men. It then knocks this down right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A curse of חוה has to be something unique to women. The ייחוד ban applies equally to a man, who may not be alone with women. So it cannot count as a special curse on women.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a suggestion that will be rejected)
Seclusion, a man and woman being alone together

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the גמרא's conclusion. The word אילימא signals that this suggestion is about to be rejected.

phrases.english: If you say it is because seclusion is forbidden to her,
seclusion is forbidden to him as well.
phrases.notes: The ban goes both ways, so it is not a unique curse on women.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers and rejects a first answer to the question of Step 35.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The suggested definition of מנודה as the ייחוד prohibition.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ייחוד ban applies to men too, so it cannot be a curse given only to women.

steps.title: It means she may not marry two husbands
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that 'cut off from all people' means a woman is forbidden to two husbands.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means she is forbidden to two men.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its real answer: a woman may be married to only one man at a time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fits the requirement of being unique to women. In the law of the תורה, a man may marry more than one wife, but a woman may not have two husbands. So she is 'cut off' from every man except her husband.
steps.whatToRemember: מנודה מכל אדם means a woman can be married to only one man, while a man may marry more than one woman.

phrases.english: Rather, it means she is forbidden to two (husbands).
phrases.notes: A man, by contrast, may marry two wives.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer of Step 36 with the accepted definition.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The curse is that a woman may not be married to two men, unlike a man.

steps.title: A ברייתא gives a different list of three curses
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists three different added curses: growing long hair like לילית, sitting while urinating like an animal, and being beneath her husband during relations.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: She grows her hair long like לילית, she sits and urinates like an animal, and she serves as a pillow for her husband.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that fills in the missing three curses differently from רב דימי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב דימי's three curses were about social restrictions. The ברייתא's three are physical traits of women. Both are trying to complete the count of ten curses.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא
לילית, a female demon described with long hair

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita:
She grows her hair long like Lilit,
and she sits and urinates like an animal,
and she becomes a pillow for her husband.
phrases.notes: Meaning her position beneath him during relations.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different set of three curses in place of רב דימי's set.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The three added curses are long hair, sitting to urinate, and being beneath the husband.

steps.title: Why doesn't the other opinion count these?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב דימי did not list the ברייתא's three curses.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one (why doesn't he count these)?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the first opinion did not include these three traits. This short question sets up the answer that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are real physical facts about women, so it seems they should count as curses. The גמרא wants to know why רב דימי chose other items instead.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one? (Why does the other opinion disagree?)

phrases.english: And the other (Sage)?
phrases.notes: Why doesn't רב דימי count these as curses?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why the earlier opinion left out the ברייתא's list.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רב דימי did not count the ברייתא's three traits as curses.

steps.title: These traits are praise, not curses
steps.stepSummary: The other opinion holds that these three traits are praiseworthy for a woman.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are praise for her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב דימי sees these traits as good things, so they cannot be curses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sitting to urinate is modest, and her position during relations is more comfortable and dignified. So the disagreement is not about the facts. It is about whether these facts are a curse or a praise.

phrases.english: These are praise for her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 39.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב דימי holds these traits are praiseworthy, so he does not count them as curses.

steps.title: רבי חייא: we learn modesty and gentleness from animals
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא explains a פסוק in איוב: we learn modesty from the mule, which crouches to urinate, and gentle courtship from the rooster.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי חייא said: What is meant by the פסוק 'Who teaches us by the beasts of the earth, and makes us wiser by the birds of the sky'? 'Teaches us by the beasts' refers to the female mule, which crouches and urinates. 'Makes us wiser by the birds of the sky' refers to the rooster, which first appeases its mate and then mates with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבי חייא's teaching to prove that these behaviors are praiseworthy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the פסוק says we should learn from the mule crouching to urinate, then sitting to urinate is a good, modest trait. The rooster lesson about appeasing first fits the idea that the woman's role in relations is treated with consideration. This supports the claim of Step 40 that these are praise, not curses.

keyTerms.meaning: What is meant by what is written?

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's three 'curses' are seen by the other opinion as praise. רבי חייא's lesson from the mule shows that modesty in urinating is praiseworthy.
steps.whyThisMatters: This passage is a source for learning good manners (דרך ארץ) from the natural world: modesty from the mule and consideration for one's spouse from the rooster.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Hiyya said: What is that which is written:
"Who teaches us by the beasts of the earth
phrases.notes: איוב 35:11

phrases.english: and makes us wiser by the birds of the sky"?
"Who teaches us by the beasts": this is the female mule,
which crouches and urinates.
phrases.notes: A lesson in modesty.

phrases.english: "And makes us wiser by the birds of the sky": this is the rooster,
which first appeases (its mate) and afterward mates with it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides support for the claim that these traits are praise.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the ברייתא's traits, especially crouching to urinate, are praiseworthy.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי חייא's reading of איוב 35:11, which teaches that we learn modesty from the mule and gentle courtship from the rooster.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: Good behavior can be learned from animals
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says that even without the תורה, we could learn modesty from the cat, not stealing from the ant, faithfulness from the dove, and gentle courtship from the rooster.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: If the תורה had not been given, we would have learned modesty from the cat, not stealing from the ant, and avoiding forbidden relationships from the dove. We would have learned proper marital conduct from the rooster, which first wins over the hen and only then mates with her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second teaching, similar to רבי חייא's, that animals show us proper behavior. It ends with the rooster, which ties back to the idea of gentle courtship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each animal shows one good trait. The cat covers its waste, which is modesty. The ant does not take another ant's food, which is honesty. The dove stays with one partner, which is faithfulness. The rooster appeases before mating, which is דרך ארץ. This supports the earlier claim that a gentle, considerate approach in marriage is praiseworthy.

keyTerms.meaning: If not for / had it not been

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a well-known teaching. It shows that basic decency is something a person can see in nature, even before learning it from the תורה.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
If the Torah had not been given,
we would have learned modesty from the cat,
phrases.notes: The cat covers its waste.

phrases.english: and not stealing from the ant,
phrases.notes: An ant does not take another ant's grain.

phrases.english: and avoiding forbidden relationships from the dove.
phrases.notes: The dove stays faithful to its partner.

phrases.english: Proper marital conduct from the rooster —
which first appeases and only afterwards mates.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אִילְמָלֵא לֹא נִיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel teaching to רבי חייא's lesson from the mule and rooster. It widens the list of animals we learn from.
steps.raayaObject: That gentle courtship and modesty are praiseworthy traits
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's teaching about learning conduct from animals
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even without the תורה, proper conduct could be learned from animals: modesty from the cat, honesty from the ant, faithfulness from the dove, and gentle courtship (דרך ארץ) from the rooster.

steps.title: How does the rooster appease the hen?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the rooster actually does to win over the hen.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how does it appease her?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short clarifying question about רבי יוחנן's last example. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן said the rooster 'appeases' first, but he did not explain what that means. The גמרא wants a concrete picture of this courtship.

phrases.english: And how does it appease her?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the word מפייס in רבי יוחנן's statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the rooster's 'appeasing' of the hen actually consists of

steps.title: The rooster's promise of a coat
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, quoting רב, explains: before mating, the rooster 'promises' to buy the hen a long coat. Afterwards, he 'swears' he would buy it if he only had the means.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: This is what the rooster says to her: 'I will buy you a coat that reaches down to your feet.' Afterwards he says to her: 'May the crest of this rooster fall off if he has the money and does not buy it for you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a playful picture. Before mating, the rooster's spread wings are like a promise of a coat. Afterwards, his lowered head is like an apology that he cannot afford it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rooster speaks kindly and makes the hen feel valued before mating. Afterwards he does not ignore her. He shows that his promise was sincere and that only poverty stops him. This is the 'appeasing' that teaches proper marital conduct.
steps.whatToRemember: The rooster models דרך ארץ: speak kindly and win over your spouse first, and stay caring afterwards.
steps.confusionAlert: The rooster does not actually talk. רב is describing its body language: spreading its wings before mating and bowing its head afterwards. He reads these movements as if they were words.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said,
this is what it says to her:
phrases.notes: Before mating, it spreads its wings.

phrases.english: I will buy you a coat
that reaches down to your feet,
afterwards it says to her:
phrases.notes: After mating, it bows its head.

phrases.english: may the crest of this rooster fall off

phrases.aramaic: אִי אִית לֵיהּ וְלָא זָבֵינְנָא לִיךְ.
phrases.english: if he has the means and does not buy it for you.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב, הָכִי קָאָמַר לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of how the rooster appeases the hen.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The rooster 'promises' a long coat before mating, and afterwards 'swears' he would buy it if he could afford it.
